01 / THE DEPENDENCIES

Two bounds. One local density theorem.

  1. Greedy stretch and girth

    Process edges by nondecreasing weight. Add an edge exactly when no earlier path meets the stretch threshold. Tie-breaking is explicit.

    Claims 14, 15, 18 and corrected 19 · initial Lean proofs
  2. Small dense subgraphs

    The density increment theorem and the Moore bound produce the new sparsity exponent. The density increment is a substantial external dependency and has not been formalized here.

    Theorems 9, 11, 13 and Lemma 16 · open
  3. Cluster contraction and charging

    Lift short cluster cycles to the original graph, then combine the density bound with the hierarchical charging argument of Borradaile–Le–Wulff-Nilsen.

    Claims 22–23 and Lemma 24 · open
  4. The conditional lower bound

    High-girth components with fewer than binomial(h,2) edges exclude Kₕ minors. Every low-stretch unweighted spanner must keep all edges.

    Theorem 7 and lower half of Theorem 13 · girth-conjecture dependency
What the verification labels mean

Compilation, allowed-axiom auditing, independent kernel replay, exact-commit CI, semantic review and the final skeptical audit are distinct checks. Supporting lemmas and conditional reductions never count as completion of a main theorem. No new axioms, sorry placeholders, unchecked native decisions or hidden hypotheses are accepted.

03 / EXPLICIT CORRECTION LOG

Keep the exact threshold.

Claim 19: a missing additive term

The source constructs a greedy spanner at t=(1+sε)(2k−1), then claims weighted girth > (1+sε)2k. The general greedy theorem supplies weighted girth > t+1=2k+sε(2k−1). These differ by sε. The triangle family above shows the larger claim is false.

Repair. Retain t+1. For k≥1, g≥0, ε≥0 and s≥4g, the corrected threshold satisfies t+1≥(1+2gε)2k, which is the upper bound on the lifted cluster-cycle weight in Claim 23. Thus the numerical contradiction survives with the adjusted constant. The remaining cluster construction and charging proof are still open.

Source: PDF pages 8 and 11. The original Claim 19 below is retained verbatim for fidelity; this correction overrides its mathematical interpretation.

Lower-bound domain: h must be at least 3

The proof of Theorem 13 says its lower bound holds for every positive h and proposes trees when h is bounded. This case requires h≥3. A K₂-minor-free graph is edgeless, while every nontrivial tree has a K₂ minor. The asymptotic lower bound for large h is unaffected.

Lightness need not dominate sparsity for an individual weighted graph

The opening sentence of Section 1.1 is false with the definitions immediately above it. Take a unit-weight K₄ and join a fifth vertex by a weight-10 bridge. Sparsity is 7/5; total weight is 16 and MST weight is 13, so lightness is 16/13 < 7/5. Every edge is a unique shortest path. This local introductory statement should be removed or qualified; no main upper bound relies on it here.

These are source-checked mathematical clarifications. The finite graph calculation is not represented as a Lean-certified theorem.

External dependencies stay visible

Theorem 9 cites Postle's density increment theorem. The cited 2020 preprint was withdrawn as obsolete for its coloring application; the paper itself explains this and points to the subsequent Delcourt–Postle work. This is not treated as an axiom or assumed proved in Lean. Lemma 24's charging construction also remains an explicit dependency.

Multiplicative Spanners in Minor-Free Graphs

Greg Bodwin Thanks: University of Michigan, MI, USA. Email: bodwin@umich.edu.    Gary Hoppenworth Thanks: University of Michigan, MI, USA. Email: garytho@umich.edu.    Zihan Tan Thanks: Rutgers University, NJ, USA. Email: zihantan1993@gmail.com.

In FOCS 2017, Borradaille, Le, and Wulff-Nilsen addressed a long-standing open problem by proving that minor-free graphs have light spanners. Specifically, they proved that every KhK_{h}-minor-free graph has a (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanner of lightness Oε​(h​log⁡h)O_{{\varepsilon}}(h\sqrt{\log h}), hence constant when hh and ε{\varepsilon} are regarded as constants.

We extend this result by showing that a more expressive size/stretch tradeoff is available. Specifically: for any positive integer kk, every nn-node, KhK_{h}-minor-free graph has a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner with sparsity

O⁡(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h),O\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right),

and a (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner with lightness

Oε​(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h).O_{{\varepsilon}}\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right).

We further prove that this exponent 2k+1\frac{2}{k+1} is best possible, assuming the girth conjecture. At a technical level, our proofs leverage the recent improvements by Postle (2020) to the remarkable density increment theorem for minor-free graphs.

1 Introduction

Given an input graph GG, a kk-spanner is a sparse subgraph HH whose shortest path distances agree with those of GG up to a small multiplicative factor kk, called the stretch. Spanners were introduced by Peleg and Schaffer [PS89] after being used implicitly in prior work in distributed computing [PU87, PU89], and have since found widespread application in network design, graph algorithms, etc (see survey [ABS+20]).

A primary goal of research on spanners is to optimize the worst-case tradeoff between stretch and size. There are two popular ways to measure the size of a spanner:

  • •

    The first is by its sparsity, |E⁡(H)|/n|E(H)|/n (where nn is the number of vertices in the input graph). This measure arises e.g. when the goal is to store the spanner in few bits of memory, or when running algorithms on the spanner whose runtime is sensitive to the spanner sparsity.

  • •

    The second is by its total weight w⁡(H)w(H). Since w⁡(H)w(H) can generally be unbounded, it is popular to normalize the spanner weight by the weight of a minimum spanning tree (MST) of the input graph: the lightness of a spanner HH of a graph GG is the quantity

    ℓ⁡(H∣G):=w⁡(H)w​(MST​(G)).\ell(H\mid G):=\frac{w(H)}{w(\texttt{MST}(G))}.

1.1 Sparsity and Lightness in General Graphs

The lightness of a graph is always at least as large as its sparsity, and in general it could be much higher. However, in some sense this difference can be bounded. Let us restrict attention to nn-node metric graphs, in which every edge is the unique shortest path between its endpoints, which is the natural setting for spanner problems (i.e., non-metric edges can be removed without affecting the distances in GG). Here, the bounds are:

Theorem 1 (Folklore).

Every nn-node metric graph GG has sparsity O⁡(n)O(n) and lightness O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}).

For the upper bound on lightness, note that the graph GG has at most n2n^{2} edges, each of weight at most w​(MST​(G))w(\texttt{MST}(G)). For the lower bound, consider an nn-node path with edges of weight 11, augmented with all additional edges where the weight of (u,v)(u,v) is set to their distance along the path minus ε{\varepsilon}. Although this bound is tight, it has been known since the seminal work of Khuller, Raghavachari, and Young [KRY95] that one can improve lightness to O⁡(n)O(n), matching sparsity, by paying a (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon}) factor in stretch:

Theorem 2 ([KRY95]).

For any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0, every nn-node graph GG has a (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanner with lightness Oε​(n)O_{{\varepsilon}}(n).11 1 We use OεO_{{\varepsilon}} notation to hide polynomial dependencies on ε−1{\varepsilon}^{-1}.

Once this initial upper bound is established, it is then natural to ask whether one can pay an even higher stretch to improve the O⁡(n)O(n) sparsity and lightness dependence. After a long line of work [ADD+93, CDNS92, ENS15a, CWN18, FS20, LS23, Bod25, BF25], especially on the side of lightness, the following tradeoffs is now known:

Theorem 3 ([ADD+93, CWN18, LS23, Bod25]).

For any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and positive integer kk, every nn-node graph has a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner with sparsity O⁡(n1/k)O(n^{1/k}) and a (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner with lightness Oε​(n1/k)O_{{\varepsilon}}(n^{1/k}).

This sparsity bound is known to be best possible, assuming the girth conjecture [Erd63]. For lightness, the n1/kn^{1/k} dependence is tight assuming the girth conjecture as well. The exact (hidden) dependence on ε{\varepsilon} remains open, but it was recently proved that the ε{\varepsilon}-dependence is not entirely removable [BF25].

1.2 Sparsity and Lightness in Minor-Free Graphs

An important special case for spanners is that where the input is KhK_{h}-minor-free; this arises as a technical tool in approximation algorithms for the Traveling Salesman Problem [RS98, AGK+98, BDT14, GS02, DHK11], and in some sense it generalizes the well-studied setting of Euclidean input graphs (see book [NS07]). A KhK_{h}-minor-free graph is already guaranteed to be quite sparse, and therefore comparably light:

Theorem 4 ([Kos82, AKS23]).

Every nn-node, KhK_{h}-minor-free metric graph has sparsity O⁡(h​log⁡h)O(h\sqrt{\log h}) and lightness O⁡(n​h​log⁡h)O(nh\sqrt{\log h}).22 2 For a gradual exposition of the proof and development of ideas in this theorem, we recommend the excellent recent blog post by Hung Le [Le22].

Is is natural to ask, like for general graphs, whether one can remove the nn-dependence from the lightness bound by paying an extra (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon}) factor in the stretch. This was a long-standing open question: it was first asked in 2002 by Grigni and Sissokho [GS02], and then conjectured to be possible in 2012 by Grigni and Hung [GH12] (who showed that (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon}) stretch can be used to improve the dependence to log⁡n\log n). The result was finally achieved in a remarkable FOCS 2017 paper by Borradaille, Le, and Wulff-Nilsen:

Theorem 5 ([BLWN17]).

For any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0, every nn-node, KhK_{h}-minor-free graph has a (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanner with lightness Oε​(h​log⁡h)O_{{\varepsilon}}(h\sqrt{\log h}).

Analogous to the work on general graphs, a natural next step after this theorem is to investigate the full tradeoff between stretch and sparsity/lightness for minor-free graphs. That is the subject of the current paper. We prove the following new bounds:

Theorem 6 (Main Result, Upper Bounds).

For any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and positive integer kk, every nn-node, KhK_{h}-minor-free graph has a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner with sparsity

O⁡(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h),O\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right),

and a (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner with lightness

Oε​(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h).O_{{\varepsilon}}\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right).

The exponent 2k+1\frac{2}{k+1} in Theorem 6 might look surprising; at first, one might guess that the exponent would be 1k\frac{1}{k} to match Theorem 3. However, we further prove that this is indeed the correct exponent for minor-free graphs:

Theorem 7 (Main Result, Lower Bounds).

Assuming the girth conjecture [Erd63], there are nn-node KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs for which any (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner has sparsity and lightness

Ω⁡(h2k+1).\Omega\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\right).

Our upper and lower bounds differ by polylog ​h\text{polylog }h factors. It seems unlikely that these factors can be removed entirely from the upper bound, since we know that a log⁡h\sqrt{\log h} factor is truly necessary in the sparsity and lightness bounds for minor-free graphs. However, it would be interesting to have this polylog ​h\text{polylog }h dependence degrade with the stretch. We conjecture that the following improvement to our bounds will be possible:

Conjecture 8.

For any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and positive integer kk, every nn-node, KhK_{h}-minor-free graph has a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner with sparsity

O⁡((h⋅polylog ​h)2k+1),O\left(\left(h\cdot\text{polylog }h\right)^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\right),

and a (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner with lightness

Oε​((h⋅polylog ​h)2k+1).O_{{\varepsilon}}\left(\left(h\cdot\text{polylog }h\right)^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\right).

The advantage of this conjecture over our main result would be that it would allow spanners of truly constant sparsity/lightness (even as a function of hh), in exchange for stretch O⁡(log⁡h)O(\log h). This would be a satisfying analog to the important special case of spanners with constant sparsity/lightness and stretch O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) for general graphs.

1.3 Techniques: A Density Increment Theorem for Minor-Free Graphs

A density increment theorem for minor-free graphs is a result that guarantees that every minor-free graph has a relatively dense subgraph. Density increment theorems for minor-free graphs have emerged as a powerful tool in recent progress on Hadwiger’s Conjecture [Pos20, DP25a, NPS23]. This paper makes the point that they may be far more broadly applicable to algorithmic and combinatorial analysis of minor-free graphs as well.

For intuition, let us revisit the bound of O⁡(h​log⁡h)O(h\sqrt{\log h}) on the sparsity of minor-free graphs. One can get a nearly-matching lower bound by considering the disjoint union of nh−1\frac{n}{h-1} cliques of size h−1h-1 each: this has sparsity Ω⁡(h)\Omega(h), and is clearly KhK_{h}-minor-free. The actual tight lower bound is only slightly more involved than that; it is a disjoint union of many carefully-designed small graphs that are each nearly a clique.

These constructions based on disjoint unions will contain “clustered” parts of the graph, i.e., very small subgraphs whose average degree is roughly the same as the original graph. The Density Increment Theorem says, in some sense, that this is not a coincidence: all nearly-tight lower bound graphs must have this structure.

Theorem 9 (Density Increment Theorem [Pos20], reformulated).
33 3 The cited work has been withdrawn from arXiv, since the goal of this theorem in the paper was to prove an O⁡(t​log⁡log6​t)O(t\log\log^{6}t) bound on Hadwiger’s conjecture and an improved bound of O⁡(t​log⁡log​t)O(t\log\log t) was proved by the author and Delcourt in a subsequent work [DP25b] via a similar approach. However, the stated Density Increment Theorem still holds. See also the remark in [DP25b] (the paragraph after Theorem 2.2).

Let GG be a KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with average degree dd. Then GG contains a subgraph on at most (h2/d)⋅polylog ​h(h^{2}/d)\cdot\text{polylog }h vertices, with average degree at least dpolylog ​h\frac{d}{\text{polylog }h}.

For analyzing spanner sparsity, the density increment theorem yields a remarkably simple proof. Our strategy is to use the standard greedy spanner algorithm [ADD+93] to construct a KhK_{h}-minor-free spanner HH with high girth. We can then use the density increment theorem to pass to a very small subgraph H′⊆HH^{\prime}\subseteq H of comparable sparsity, which still has high girth. The standard Moore bounds, which limit the maximum possible density of a high-girth graph, then yield our desired theorem when applied to H′H^{\prime}. The gap of polylog ​h\text{polylog }h between Theorem 6 and Conjecture 8 comes entirely from the polylog ​h\text{polylog }h loss in the density increment theorem itself.

For analyzing spanner lightness, the density increment theorem is still useful, but the proof is necessarily more involved. We again start by using the greedy algorithm to construct a KhK_{h}-minor-free spanner HH with high weighted girth (see Definition 4.1). However, we cannot simply use the density increment theorem to pass to a small subgraph H′H^{\prime}: although we could bound the lightness of H′H^{\prime}, we do not have a good way to compare MST​(H′)\texttt{MST}(H^{\prime}) and MST​(H)\texttt{MST}(H), so this would not reveal much about the lightness of HH. Instead, we need to dip into the techniques of Borradaille, Le, and Wulff-Nilsen [BLWN17] for proving the initial bound on minor-free spanner lightness in Theorem 5.

1.4 Other Related Work

Spanners have been extensively studied in Euclidean graphs, where the nodes are embedded in Euclidean space, there are all possible edges among nodes, and the weight of each edge (u,v)(u,v) set to the Euclidean distance w⁡(u,v):=‖u−v‖2w(u,v):=\|u-v\|_{2}. We refer to the book by Narasimhan and Smid for a thorough account [NS07]. The following near-optimal tradeoffs were recently determined by Le and Solomon [LS22]:

Theorem 10 (Constant Sparsity/Lightness Spanners for Euclidean Graphs [LS22]).

For any constant ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and constant integer d≥2d\geq 2, every dd-dimensional Euclidean graph has a spanner with ⋅(1+ε)\cdot(1+{\varepsilon}) stretch, sparsity O⁡(ε−d+1)O\left({\varepsilon}^{-d+1}\right), and lightness O⁡(ε−d​log⁡ε−1)O\left({\varepsilon}^{-d}\log{\varepsilon}^{-1}\right). These tradeoffs are best possible, up to the factor of log⁡ε−1\log{\varepsilon}^{-1} in lightness.

One can again ask whether it is possible to pay more stretch in exchange for a better dependence on ε{\varepsilon} or dd. This question has been studied, but so far remains open. Aronov et al. [ADBC+08] showed that one can pay a much larger stretch of O⁡(n/k)O(n/k) in exchange for an extremely sparse spanner with number of edges |E⁡(H)|≤n−1+k|E(H)|\leq n-1+k. Work of Filtser and Neiman [FN22] (c.f. Remark 1) implied that one can pay O⁡(t)O(t) stretch for sparsity and lightness exp⁡(d/t2)⋅polylog ​n\exp(d/t^{2})\cdot\text{polylog }n. However, a general tradeoff remains elusive.

Euclidean graphs are naturally generalized by doubling metrics, where analogous sparsity/lightness bounds for (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanners, e.g. [Got15, BLWN19, FS20]. Extending these results to higher stretch would be interesting as well.

2 Preliminaries

Graph Notation.

Given a graph GG and an edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), we let G−eG-e denote the graph obtained by removing ee from GG. We denote the weight of an edge ee in GG by w⁡(e)w(e). Given a pair of vertices s,t∈V⁡(G)s,t\in V(G), we let distG​(s,t)\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(s,t) denote the weighted distance between ss and tt in graph GG.

Our proofs will require a standard theorem in the graph spanner literature that bounds the number of edges in large girth graphs.

Theorem 11 (Moore bounds).

For all positive integers k,nk,n, every nn-vertex graph with girth >2​k>2k has at most O⁡(n1+1/k)O(n^{1+1/k}) edges.

Erdős conjectured that this upper bound is tight; this is frequently referred to as the girth conjecture.

Conjecture 12 (Erdős girth conjecture).

The Moore bounds are tight. That is, for every positive integer kk and sufficiently large positive integer nn, there exists an nn-vertex graph with girth >2​k>2k and Ω⁡(n1+1/k)\Omega(n^{1+1/k}) edges.

3 Sparse Multiplicative Spanners in Minor-Free Graphs

In this section we will prove that KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs have sparse multiplicative spanners.

Theorem 13 (Minor-Free Spanner Sparsity).

For all positive integers k,h,nk,h,n, every KhK_{h}-minor-free weighted graph on nn vertices admits a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-multiplicative spanner with number of edges

O⁡(n⋅h2k+1⋅polylog ​h)O\left(n\cdot h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right)

Moreover, this bound is tight up to polylog ​h\text{polylog }h factors under the girth conjecture.

Let GG be an nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free weighted graph, and let kk be a positive integer. We will construct a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner H⊆GH\subseteq G using a greedy strategy that is standard in the area. We first present the construction of HH, and then analyze its correctness and size.

Construction of HH.

We may assume without loss of generality that for each edge (u,v)∈E⁡(G)(u,v)\in E(G), w⁡((u,v))=distG​(u,v)w((u,v))=\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v) by removing edges from GG that do not satisfy this condition. Initially, let H←(V,∅)H\leftarrow(V,\emptyset). For each edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E in order of non-decreasing weight, if distH​(u,v)>(2​k−1)⋅distG​(u,v)\textnormal{{dist}}_{H}(u,v)>(2k-1)\cdot\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v), then add edge (u,v)(u,v) to HH. After iterating through all edges in EE, return HH.

We quickly verify that HH is indeed a multiplicative spanner of GG.

Claim 14 (Correctness).

HH is a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner of GG.

Proof.

This proof follows from a standard argument that can be attributed to [ADD+93]. For each edge (u,v)∈E⁡(G)(u,v)\in E(G), we know that either distH​(u,v)≤(2​k−1)⋅distG​(u,v)\textnormal{{dist}}_{H}(u,v)\leq(2k-1)\cdot\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v) or (u,v)∈E⁡(H)(u,v)\in E(H). Since w⁡((u,v))=distG​(u,v)w((u,v))=\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v), we conclude that for each edge (u,v)∈E⁡(G)(u,v)\in E(G), distH​(u,v)≤(2​k−1)⋅distG​(u,v)\textnormal{{dist}}_{H}(u,v)\leq(2k-1)\cdot\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v). Combining this fact with the triangle inequality, it follows that for all s,t∈V⁡(G)s,t\in V(G), distH​(s,t)≤(2​k−1)⋅distG​(s,t)\textnormal{{dist}}_{H}(s,t)\leq(2k-1)\cdot\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(s,t). ∎

Size Analysis of HH.

Next we prove our desired upper bound on the number of edges in HH. We begin with the following observation about HH.

Claim 15.

HH is a KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k.

Proof.

Since GG is KhK_{h}-minor-free, HH is as well. We can prove HH has girth >2​k>2k using a standard argument that we can attribute to [ADD+93]. Let CC be a simple cycle in HH. We will show |C|>2​k|C|>2k. Consider the edge e∈Ce\in C with highest weight w⁡(e)w(e). The path between the endpoints of edge ee in C−eC-e has length at most (|C|−1)⋅w⁡(e)(|C|-1)\cdot w(e). By the construction of HH, we would not add edge ee to HH if (|C|−1)⋅w⁡(e)≤(2​k−1)⋅w⁡(e)(|C|-1)\cdot w(e)\leq(2k-1)\cdot w(e). We conclude that |C|>2​k|C|>2k. ∎

Now applying the density increment theorem, we obtain the following general theorem about the number of edges in minor-free graphs with large girth.

Lemma 16.

For all positive integers k,h,nk,h,n, every nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k has at most O⁡(n⋅h2k+1⋅polylog ​h)O(n\cdot h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h) edges.

Proof.

Let HH be an nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k and average degree dd. Then by the Density Increment Theorem, there exists a subgraph H′⊆HH^{\prime}\subseteq H with at most |V⁡(H′)|≤(h2/d)⋅polylog ​h|V(H^{\prime})|\leq(h^{2}/d)\cdot\text{polylog }h vertices and at least |E⁡(H′)|≥|V⁡(H′)|⋅dpolylog ​h|E(H^{\prime})|\geq|V(H^{\prime})|\cdot\frac{d}{\text{polylog }h}. Subgraph H′H^{\prime} has girth >2​k>2k, so by Theorem 11,

dpolylog ​h⋅|V⁡(H′)|≤|E⁡(H′)|≤O⁡(|V⁡(H′)|1+1/k).\frac{d}{\text{polylog }h}\cdot|V(H^{\prime})|\leq|E(H^{\prime})|\leq O(|V(H^{\prime})|^{1+1/k}).

Plugging in |V⁡(H′)|≤(h2/d)⋅polylog ​h|V(H^{\prime})|\leq(h^{2}/d)\cdot\text{polylog }h yields the inequality

dpolylog ​h\displaystyle\frac{d}{\text{polylog }h} ≤(h2/d)1/k⋅polylog ​h,\displaystyle\leq(h^{2}/d)^{1/k}\cdot\text{polylog }h,

and solving for dd gives us

d≤h2/(k+1)⋅polylog ​h.d\leq h^{2/(k+1)}\cdot\text{polylog }h.

∎

We can now complete the proof of Theorem 13.

See 13

Proof.

By Claim 14, Claim 15, and Lemma 16, subgraph HH is a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner of GG of size |E⁡(H)|=O⁡(n⋅h2/(k+1)⋅polylog ​h)|E(H)|=O(n\cdot h^{2/(k+1)}\cdot\text{polylog }h). What remains is to prove that this upper bound is tight up to polylog ​h\text{polylog }h factors under the girth conjecture (Conjecture 12).

Formally, we will show that for all positive integers k,h,k,h, and for sufficiently large nn, there exists an nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graph GG that does not admit a (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner HH of GG of size |E⁡(H)|=Ω⁡(n⋅h2/(k+1))|E(H)|=\Omega(n\cdot h^{2/(k+1)}). If h=O⁡(1)h=O(1), then we can let GG be a tree. Every spanner HH of GG must include every edge of the tree, so |E⁡(H)|=Ω⁡(n)|E(H)|=\Omega(n), as desired. Otherwise, if hh is sufficiently large, then by the girth conjecture there exists a graph G∗G^{*} with |V⁡(G∗)|=Θ⁡(h2​k/(k+1))|V(G^{*})|=\Theta(h^{2k/(k+1)}) vertices, |E⁡(G∗)|≥Ω⁡(h2)|E(G^{*})|\geq\Omega(h^{2}) edges, and girth >2​k>2k. Moreover, we can guarantee that |E⁡(G∗)|<(h2)|E(G^{*})|<{h\choose 2} by removing edges from G∗G^{*}.

We compose our final lower bound graph GG by unioning n/|V⁡(G∗)|=Θ⁡(nh2​k/(k+1))n/|V(G^{*})|=\Theta\left(\frac{n}{h^{2k/(k+1)}}\right) disjoint copies of graph G∗G^{*}. Graph GG will have Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) vertices (we can ensure |V⁡(G)|=n|V(G)|=n by deleting or adding vertices as needed). Graph GG has girth >2​k>2k and is KhK_{h}-minor-free, since every connected component of GG has fewer than (h2){h\choose 2} edges. Since graph GG has girth >2​k>2k, every (2​k−1)(2k-1)-spanner HH of GG must contain every edge in GG, i.e., H=GH=G. We conclude that

|E⁡(H)|=|E⁡(G)|=Θ⁡(nh2​k/(k+1))⋅h2=Θ⁡(n⋅h2/(k+1)),|E(H)|=|E(G)|=\Theta\left(\frac{n}{h^{2k/(k+1)}}\right)\cdot h^{2}=\Theta(n\cdot h^{2/(k+1)}),

as claimed. ∎

4 Light Multiplicative Spanners in Minor-Free Graphs

In this section we will prove that KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs have multiplicative spanners with small lightness.

Theorem 17 (Minor-Free Spanner Lightness).

For all positive integers k,h,nk,h,n, and sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, every KhK_{h}-minor-free weighted graph on nn vertices admits a (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+\varepsilon)(2k-1)-multiplicative spanner with lightness

O⁡(h2k+1⋅polylog​(h)⋅1ε3​log⁡1ε).O\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog}(h)\cdot\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}^{3}}\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right).

Our proof will directly follow the proof of Borradaile, Le, and Wulff-Nilsen [BLWN17] that KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs have (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanners with lightness O⁡(h​log⁡h⋅1ε3​log⁡1ε)O\left(h\sqrt{\log h}\cdot\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}^{3}}\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right). In fact, our proof will only have two differences from their proof.

  • •

    Construction Difference: Instead of constructing a greedy (1+ε)(1+{\varepsilon})-spanner as in [BLWN17], we will construct a greedy (1+ε)​(2​k−1)(1+{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner. (Recall that a greedy spanner is a spanner constructed by the greedy strategy described in Section 3.)

  • •

    Analysis Difference: Instead of arguing that nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs have O⁡(n​h​log⁡h)O(nh\sqrt{\log h}) edges, we will apply Lemma 16 to argue that nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs with girth >2​k>2k have at most O⁡(n⋅h2k+1⋅polylog ​h)O(n\cdot h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h) edges.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free weighted graph. We may assume without loss of generality that for each edge (u,v)∈E⁡(G)(u,v)\in E(G), w⁡((u,v))=distG​(u,v)w((u,v))=\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v) by removing edges from GG that do not satisfy this condition. Let k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} be a positive integer, and let ε∈ℝ+{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} be a sufficiently small real number. For ease of presentation, we will construct a (1+s⋅ε)​(2​k−1)(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner H⊆GH\subseteq G, for a sufficiently large constant s∈ℤ+s\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}. This will not affect our bounds in Theorem 17 because we can always decrease ε{\varepsilon} by a 1s\frac{1}{s} factor to remove the dependency on ss in our distortion bounds.

Construction of HH.

We define our light spanner HH to be a greedy (1+s⋅ε)​(2​k−1)(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner of GG. Initially, let H←(V,∅)H\leftarrow(V,\emptyset). For each edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E in order of non-decreasing weight, if distH​(u,v)>(1+s⋅ε)​(2​k−1)⋅distG​(u,v)\textnormal{{dist}}_{H}(u,v)>(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})(2k-1)\cdot\textnormal{{dist}}_{G}(u,v), then add edge (u,v)(u,v) to HH. After iterating through all edges in EE, return HH.

We will prove some basic properties of subgraph HH before proceeding with the lightness upper bound in the following section.

Claim 18 (Correctness).

HH is a (1+s⋅ε)​(2​k−1)(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})(2k-1)-spanner of GG.

Proof.

Follows from an identical argument as in 14. ∎

We now define the notion of weighted girth, which generalizes standard notion of graph girth to the weighted setting.

Definition 4.1 (Normalized Cycle Weight and Weighted Girth [ENS15b]).

We define the normalized weight of a cycle CC in GG to be

w∗​(C):=w⁡(C)maxe∈C⁡w⁡(e).w^{*}(C):=\frac{w(C)}{\max_{e\in C}w(e)}.

The weighted girth of GG is defined as the minimum normalized weight w∗​(C)w^{*}(C) of any cycle CC in graph GG.

By a standard argument in the light spanner literature (see, e.g., [ENS15b, Bod25]), subgraph HH has large weighted girth.

Claim 19 (cf. Lemma 3.2 of [Bod25]).

HH is a KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with weighted girth >(1+s⋅ε)⋅2​k>(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})\cdot 2k.

Proof.

Since GG is KhK_{h}-minor-free, subgraph HH is KhK_{h}-minor-free as well. Additionally, by Lemma 3.2 of [Bod25], since HH is a greedy spanner of GG with approximation parameter (1+s⋅ε)⋅2​k(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})\cdot 2k, subgraph HH has weighted girth >(1+s⋅ε)⋅2​k>(1+s\cdot{\varepsilon})\cdot 2k, as claimed. ∎

We note that if HH has weighted girth >t>t, then HH has girth >t>t as well. Consequently, 19 implies that HH has girth >2​k>2k.

Reduction to unit-weight MST edges.

In our analysis, we can assume without loss of generality that HH has a minimum spanning tree with unit weight edges using a standard reduction in the literature [CWN18, BLWN17, Bod25]. This reduction can be summarized with the following lemma.

Lemma 20 (cf. Lemma 3.4 of [Bod25]).

Let HH be an nn-vertex KhK_{h}-minor-free graph graph with weighted girth >t>t and lightness ℓ\ell. Then there exists a KhK_{h}-minor-free graph H′H^{\prime} with O⁡(n)O(n) vertices, weighted girth >t>t, and lightness Ω⁡(ℓ)\Omega(\ell) such that HH has unit weight MST edges and every edge in HH has weight at least one.44 4 The proof of Lemma 3.4 in [Bod25] does not explicitly prove that H′H^{\prime} is KhK_{h}-minor-free. However, H′H^{\prime} is constructed by subdividing and reweighting edges in HH, which does not introduce any new clique minors into H′H^{\prime}.

For the remainder of this section, we assume that the MST of HH has weight one edges, and all edges in HH have weight at least one.

4.1 Applying the Hierarchical Clustering Analysis of [BLWN17]

In this section, we will apply the analysis of [BLWN17] to complete the proof of Theorem 17. We begin by partitioning the edge set E⁡(H)E(H) of our spanner HH in the same way as [BLWN17].

Let σh,k\sigma_{h,k} denote the largest average degree of any KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k. By Lemma 16, σh,k=O⁡(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h)\sigma_{h,k}=O(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h). Let E′⊆E⁡(H)E^{\prime}\subseteq E(H) be the edges in HH with weights in the range [1,1/ε)[1,1/{\varepsilon}). We begin with the following simple observation.

Claim 21 (cf. equation 3 of [BLWN17]).

w⁡(E′)=O⁡(σh,k⋅n/ε)=O⁡(σh,k⋅ε−1⋅w⁡(MST))w(E^{\prime})=O(\sigma_{h,k}\cdot n/{\varepsilon})=O\left(\sigma_{h,k}\cdot{\varepsilon}^{-1}\cdot w(\text{MST})\right)

Proof.

We know that w⁡(MST)=n−1w(\text{MST})=n-1, by our assumption that the edges of the minimum spanning tree of GG are unit weight. Additionally, we know that |E′|≤σh,k⋅n|E^{\prime}|\leq\sigma_{h,k}\cdot n, since HH is a KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k by 19. By the definition of E′E^{\prime}, we conclude that w⁡(E′)=O⁡(σh,k⋅n/ε)=O⁡(σh,k⋅ε−1⋅w⁡(MST)).w(E^{\prime})=O(\sigma_{h,k}\cdot n/{\varepsilon})=O\left(\sigma_{h,k}\cdot{\varepsilon}^{-1}\cdot w(\text{MST})\right). ∎

We now develop some of the notation and definitions used in the analysis of the light spanner in [BLWN17]. Let Eji⊆E⁡(H)E^{i}_{j}\subseteq E(H) be the set of edges in HH with weights in the range [2jεi,2j+1εi)\left[\frac{2^{j}}{{\varepsilon}^{i}},\frac{2^{j+1}}{{\varepsilon}^{i}}\right) for every i∈ℤ+i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} and every j∈[0,⌈log⁡1ε⌉]j\in\left[0,\left\lceil\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right\rceil\right]. Proof.

Applying the lightness argument of [BLWN17].

For each j∈[0,⌈log⁡1ε⌉]j\in\left[0,\left\lceil\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right\rceil\right], the authors of [BLWN17] upper bound the lightness of edges in EjiE_{j}^{i} for all i∈ℤ+i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} using a careful charging scheme. We will black-box their charging scheme using Lemma 24 to follow.

At level ii, the clusters in 𝒞ji\mathcal{C}_{j}^{i} are clustered together using edges in Eji+1E_{j}^{i+1} to form the level i+1i+1 clusters 𝒞ji+1\mathcal{C}_{j}^{i+1}. During level ii, the authors of [BLWN17] need to carefully pay for the weights of edges in Eji+1E_{j}^{i+1} using credits stored in each cluster in 𝒞ji\mathcal{C}_{j}^{i}, while maintaining enough excess credits to pay for edges in higher levels as well. A key observation used in their proof is that cluster graph 𝒦ji\mathcal{K}_{j}^{i} is KhK_{h}-minor-free, and therefore on average each cluster in 𝒞ji\mathcal{C}_{j}^{i} is incident to O⁡(h​log⁡h)O(h\sqrt{\log h}) edges in 𝒦ji\mathcal{K}_{j}^{i}. This charging scheme analysis yields the following lemma, which is implicit in the proof of Lemma 2 in [BLWN17].

Lemma 24 (cf. Lemma 2 of [BLWN17]).

Let d∈ℝ+d\in\mathbb{R}^{+} be the largest average degree of any cluster graph 𝒦ji\mathcal{K}_{j}^{i} for j∈[0,⌈log⁡1ε⌉]j\in\left[0,\left\lceil\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right\rceil\right] and i∈ℤ+i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}.66 6 Although cluster graph 𝒦ij\mathcal{K}_{i}^{j} is defined for all i∈ℤ+i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, there are only finitely many distinct cluster graphs in the hierarchy. Thus, dd is well-defined. There exists a set of edges B⊆E⁡(H)B\subseteq E(H) such that w⁡(B)=O⁡(1ε2​w​(MST))w(B)=O\left(\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}^{2}}w(\text{MST})\right) and for every j∈[0,⌈log⁡1ε⌉]j\in\left[0,\left\lceil\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right\rceil\right],

w⁡(Jj−B)≤O⁡(dε3)​w​(MST).w\left(J_{j}-B\right)\leq O\left(\frac{d}{{\varepsilon}^{3}}\right)w(\text{MST}).

We can combine Lemma 24 with our upper bound on the sparsity of minor-free graphs with large girth in 23 to prove our light spanner upper bound.

See 17

Proof.

By 23, every cluster graph 𝒦ji\mathcal{K}_{j}^{i} is KhK_{h}-minor-free and has girth >2​k>2k. Then since σh,k\sigma_{h,k} is the largest average degree of any KhK_{h}-minor-free graph with girth >2​k>2k, every cluster graph 𝒦ji\mathcal{K}_{j}^{i} has average degree at most σh,k\sigma_{h,k}.

Then by Lemma 24, there exists a set of edges B⊆E⁡(H)B\subseteq E(H) such that

w⁡(H)=w⁡(E′)+w⁡(B)+∑j∈[0,⌈log⁡1ε⌉]w⁡(Jj−B)=O⁡(σh,kε3​log​1ε)​w​(MST).w(H)=w(E^{\prime})+w(B)+\sum_{j\in\left[0,\left\lceil\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right\rceil\right]}w(J_{j}-B)=O\left(\frac{\sigma_{h,k}}{{\varepsilon}^{3}}\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right)w(\text{MST}).

Plugging in our upper bound of σh,k=O⁡(h2k+1⋅polylog ​h)\sigma_{h,k}=O\left(h^{\frac{2}{k+1}}\cdot\text{polylog }h\right) on σh,k\sigma_{h,k} from Lemma 16 completes the proof of Theorem 17. ∎
